beneficial.summary: Cowpea fixes atmospheric nitrogen, reducing the need for fertilizer, while Maize provides structural support.
Maize harvests early, allowing slow-growing Cassava to take over the space later in the season.
Groundnut acts as a living mulch, suppressing weeds and retaining soil moisture for the tall maize stalks.

overview: Maize is the backbone of West African food security. It is versatile, growing in diverse ecological zones, and serves as a critical source of carbohydrates.
notes: Best planted at the onset of rains. Susceptible to striga weed, which legumes can help suppress.

beneficial.summary: Thrives under the partial shade of cereals like Maize and Sorghum, maximizing land use efficiency.
Intercropping with Sorghum can reduce flower thrips populations and improve overall grain yield.

overview: Known as the 'hungry season crop', Cowpea provides essential protein when other crops are yet to mature. It is incredibly drought-resistant.
notes: Avoid waterlogged soils. Its leaves, pods, and seeds are all edible.

beneficial.summary: Compatible because they compete for resources at different times; Maize is fast, Cassava is slow.
Groundnuts add nitrogen to the soil which supports the heavy nutrient demands of Cassava tubers.

overview: A woody shrub native to South America but now a staple in Nigeria. It is highly resilient to poor soils and erratic rainfall.
notes: Requires good drainage to prevent root rot. Processing is required to remove cyanogenic glycosides.

beneficial.summary: Farmers often plant maize early; the dried maize stalks later serve as stakes for the climbing yam vines.
Young yams benefit from the dappled shade provided by broad plantain leaves during early establishment.

overview: Yam is culturally significant in Nigeria, often called the 'King of Crops'. It requires deep, loose soil for tuber expansion.
notes: Mounding is essential for good formation. Staking increases yield by exposing leaves to sunlight.

beneficial.summary: Plantains provide essential shade for young cocoa seedlings, protecting them from scorching sun.
Cocoyam thrives in the moist, shady microclimate beneath the broad plantain canopy.

overview: A major source of energy in the south. Unlike bananas, plantains are typically cooked before eating.
notes: Highly susceptible to wind damage; planting in clusters helps. Requires high organic matter.

beneficial.summary: The strong scent of onions confuses pests like aphids and beetles that typically attack tomatoes.
Often intercropped due to similar water and nutrient requirements, simplifying irrigation schedules.

overview: Essential for Nigerian stews and sauces. While lucrative, it is sensitive to pests and fungal diseases.
notes: Staking is recommended to keep fruits off the ground and reduce rot. Crop rotation is vital.

beneficial.summary: Sorghum roots break up heavy soil, while groundnuts replenish the nitrogen Sorghum consumes.
Sorghum can act as a windbreak for cowpea and help manage Striga parasitic weed populations.

overview: An ancient grain perfectly adapted to hot, arid climates where maize might fail. Used for food, fodder, and brewing.
notes: Very drought tolerant. Bird attacks on grain heads can be a major challenge.

beneficial.summary: Essential for young cocoa. Plantain leaves protect delicate cocoa seedlings from direct tropical sun.
Cassava provides ground cover and quick economic returns while waiting for cocoa trees to mature.

overview: Nigeria's major non-oil export. Cocoa requires specific humid conditions and shade management to thrive.
notes: Requires careful fermentation and drying of beans. Susceptible to Black Pod disease.

beneficial.summary: Groundnut fixes nitrogen for the heavy-feeding maize, while maize provides a microclimate.
Excellent rotation partner for sorghum to break disease cycles and restore soil fertility.

overview: A dual-purpose crop providing food (nuts) and fodder (haulms) for livestock. It fixes its own nitrogen.
notes: Loose soil is required for the 'pegs' to penetrate the ground and form pods.

beneficial.summary: Onions help repel aphids and spider mites that frequently attack pepper plants.
Can be intercropped with tomatoes in small holder systems, though rotation is better for disease control.

overview: Includes both sweet and hot varieties (Scotch Bonnet). A vital spice in West African cuisine.
notes: Sensitive to waterlogging. High market value but perishable.

beneficial.summary: Its pungent smell masks the scent of tomatoes, hiding them from pests.
Serves as a natural deterrent for aphids in pepper fields.

overview: Grown extensively in the dry north using irrigation. It has a high commercial value.
notes: Requires curing after harvest to increase shelf life. Shallow rooted.

beneficial.summary: One of the few crops that yields well under the heavy shade of a plantain or cocoa canopy.
Acts as an effective ground cover in cocoa plantations, suppressing weeds.

overview: Valued for both its corms and its leafy greens (kontomire). It prefers wetter conditions than yams.
notes: Leaf blight is a major constraint. Requires minimal input compared to other tubers.
